summary: Specifies a query language for monitoring and controlling network entities, as part of the High-Level Entity Monitoring System (HEMS). It replaces RFC 1023, extends the language and adds discussion of the underlying issues. It supersedes parts of RFC 1024.

eli5.summary: It is the set of questions and commands you can send to network machines in an early management system, improved from an earlier version.

questions: what is the hems query language
how does hems monitor network entities
subtitle: A tiny stack-based query language for reading and changing the data inside a network device.

tldr.problem: A monitoring center needs one general way to ask many different network entities, such as gateways, for their data and to change some of it, without loading the entity with heavy processing.
tldr.mechanism: The entity's data is shown as a tree. A query is a sequence of ASN.1 objects run by a simple stack machine with eight commands, and the reply is a copy of the part of the tree the query visited.
tldr.outcome: It is one piece of the High-Level Entity Monitoring System (HEMS). It supersedes RFC 1023 and replaces the query-language parts of RFC 1024.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 1076 as Unknown. It obsoletes RFC 1023, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it.

sections.title: Overview and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1076 specifies a general-purpose but efficient monitoring and control language for managing network entities. A query is sent to a monitored entity and the entity sends back a response. The word query is used in the database sense: it may request information, modify data, or both.

There is no interactive conversation like in SMTP or FTP. A query is a complete request that stands on its own and gets a complete response. The language is part of HEMS, described in RFC 1021 and RFC 1022, and RFC 1024 holds the detailed number assignments.

Several design goals shape it. The query processor should put as little burden as possible on the monitored entity. The entity should not have to store the whole query, so it can answer on the fly. There are no data-reduction features such as computing averages, only data selection. And a query must not abort just because it asked for data that does not exist, so one generic query can be sent to many different hosts.
sections.eli5: You send one complete note with your questions, and you get one complete note back. The helper does not have to remember your whole note and should not have to work hard.

sections.title: The Data Tree
sections.content:
The data in an entity is modeled as a hierarchy called the data tree. An implementation does not have to store data that way, but it must present this view. A piece of data is named by the path from the root. Internal nodes are called dictionaries and leaves hold the actual data. Names are just ASN.1 tags, small integers (typically less than 30), so a name like system{ clock-msec } is compact.

The RFC's example tree has three top-level dictionaries: System, Interfaces and IPRouting. A dictionary that holds many items of one type, such as a routing table, is an array. Because a name like ip-addr would refer to the field in all entries, arrays are picked apart with filters (see the operations section).

Both queries and responses use ASN.1 <tag,length,contents> objects. A query contains opcodes, templates (names with no values), paths (a template naming exactly one node), values and filters.
sections.eli5: Everything is organized like folders inside folders. To find something you just say which folders to open, in order.

sections.title: The Eight Operations
sections.content:
The query processor is a stack machine. Objects that are not opcodes are pushed on the stack as they are read. Each opcode runs at once, so operands come first and the operator last (postfix). The stack starts with only the root dictionary. There are no stored programs, subroutines or control structures.

The eight commands are BEGIN and END (move down into a dictionary and back), GET (retrieve data), GET-ATTRIBUTES (describe the data instead), GET-RANGE (read part of an OctetString, such as memory), SET (change values), CREATE (add a table entry) and DELETE (remove entries). The reply is a copy of the parts of the tree visited, showing data after any change.

SET on a read-only item raises no error; the reply simply shows the old value. Control actions such as bringing an interface down are done by setting an item that has side effects. CREATE and DELETE work only on arrays that are meant for it.

Filters pick array entries by content. They compare an item with a constant using equal, greater-or-equal or less-or-equal, test that an item is present, and combine tests with and, or and not. An entry that lacks the tested item just fails the comparison. BEGIN, GET, GET-ATTRIBUTES, SET and DELETE accept a filter.
sections.eli5: The helper knows only eight moves: step into a folder, step back out, read, describe, read a slice, change, add and remove. A filter is like saying: only the card where the address is this one.

sections.title: Authorization
sections.content:
The RFC does not say what kind of authorization system is used, if any. The only effect is to restrict which items can be read or changed. A query runs with a level of authorization set by its environment (HEMS and the HEMP header), and each data item has some test for whether that level may access it.

The tests apply only to GET, GET-ATTRIBUTES, GET-RANGE, SET, CREATE and DELETE. They must not affect BEGIN and END, and must not hide whole dictionaries, because a failing BEGIN would end the entire query. Data the caller may not see is answered like data that does not exist: an empty object of length zero.
sections.eli5: Some papers in the cabinet are off limits. If you ask for one, you get an empty envelope, the same as if the paper were not there.

sections.title: Errors
sections.content:
Missing information is not an error. It comes back as no-value, an object with ASN.1 length 0. Other problems, such as wrong arguments on the stack or a BEGIN whose path is not a dictionary, produce an ERROR object holding errorCode, errorInstance, errorOffset, errorDescription and errorOp.

Every unfinished ASN.1 object in the reply is closed with a copy of the ERROR object, then one more copy is emitted at the end, so the error is noticed at every level of the reply. The first group of error codes, for the interpreter as a whole, starts at 100 (other error), 101 (format error), 102 (system error) and 103 (stack overflow). A query also ends once there are no more objects, and missing ENDs are filled in.
sections.eli5: Asking for something that is not there just gets you an empty answer. A real mistake gets a red flag stamped on every page of the reply.

sections.title: Extending the Set of Values
sections.content:
There are two ways to add data the language does not already know. The preferred way is to register the data and its meaning and get an ASN.1 tag assigned, so everyone can use it. The other is to wrap vendor data in a VendorSpecific dictionary.

If the vendor route is used, the private data MUST be described through GET-ATTRIBUTES. The attributes tell a person or program what a value is: its format, a long and short description, its units, its precision and its properties.
sections.eli5: If a company has its own special papers, it can put them in a clearly labeled folder, and it must include a note that explains them.
